The '''National Institute for Research in Digital Science and Technology ''' ('''Inria'''; {{Langx|fr|Institut national de recherche en sciences et technologies du numérique}}) is a French national research institution focusing on [[computer science]] and [[applied mathematics]]. It was created under the name '''French Institute for Research in Computer Science and Automation''' ('''IRIA'''; {{Langx|fr|Institut de recherche en informatique et en automatique}}) in 1967 at [[Rocquencourt, Yvelines|Rocquencourt]] near [[Paris]], part of [[Plan Calcul]]. Its first site was the historical premises of [[Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe|SHAPE]] (central command of [[NATO]] military forces), which is still used as Inria's main headquarters. In 1980, IRIA became INRIA.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/affichTexte.do?cidTexte=JORFTEXT000000519325&fastPos=1&fastReqId=515371820&categorieLien=id|title=Décret {{numéro}}79-1158 du 27 décembre 1979 Création d'un institut national de recherches en informatique et en automatique (INRIA), établissement public à caractère administratif, placé sous la tutelle du ministre de l'industrie|language=French}}</ref> Since 2011, it has been styled ''Inria''.

Inria is a [[Public Scientific and Technical Research Establishment]] (EPST) under the double supervision of the French [[Minister of National Education (France)|Ministry of National Education, Advanced Instruction and Research]] and the [[Ministry of Economy, Finance and Industry]].

==Administrative status==
[[Image:INRIA Alpes'13 - 377 Grenoble.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.1|Inria Grenoble building, 2013]]
Inria has nine research centers distributed across France (in [[Bordeaux]], [[Grenoble]]-[[Inovallée]], [[Lille]], [[Lyon]], [[Nancy, France|Nancy]], [[Paris]]-[[Rocquencourt, Yvelines|Rocquencourt]], [[Rennes]], [[Plateau de Saclay|Saclay]], and [[Sophia Antipolis]]) and one center abroad in [[Santiago de Chile]], Chile. It also contributes to academic research teams outside of those centers.

Inria Rennes is part of the joint [[Institut de recherche en informatique et systèmes aléatoires]] (IRISA) with several other entities. Inria Nancy is part of the joint [[LORIA]] (Laboratoire Lorrain de Recherche en Informatique et ses Applications) with [[CNRS]] and the [[University of Lorraine]].

Before December 2007, the three centers of Bordeaux, Lille and Saclay formed a single research center called INRIA Futurs.

In October 2010, Inria, with [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]] (now [[Sorbonne University]]) and [[Paris Diderot University]] started [[IRILL]], a center for innovation and research initiative for free software.

Inria employs 3800 people. Among them are 1300 researchers, 1000 Ph.D. students and 500 postdoctorates.

==Research==
[[Image:INRIA.JPG|thumb|right|Inria Paris-Saclay, 2014]]
[[File:INRIA 2007-02-05.jpg|thumb|alt=Two chairs on a concrete porch of a rectilinear building overlooking hills and green forest|Part of INRIA Sophia Antipolis, 2007]]
[[Image:Classroom and monitors area at INRIA Lille.jpg|thumb|right|Activity within INRIA Lille, 2010]]
[[Image:IRISA.jpg|thumb|right|INRIA Rennes in 2006, part of joint IRISA]] 
Inria does both [[Theoretical computer science|theoretical]] and applied research in computer science. In the process, it has produced many widely used programs, such as:

* [[Bigloo]], a [[Scheme (programming language)|Scheme]] implementation
* [[CADP]], a tool box for the verification of asynchronous [[concurrent systems]]
* [[Caml]], a language from the [[ML programming language|ML]] family
** [[Caml Light]] and [[OCaml]] implementations
* [[CGAL]], A C++ library for solving problems in computational geometry
* [[ChorusOS|Chorus]], microkernel-based distributed operating system
* [[CompCert]], verified C compiler for PowerPC, ARM and x86_32
* [[Contrail (software)|Contrail]]<ref name="ISGTW">{{cite web |url = http://www.isgtw.org/announcement/contrail-project-proud-present-its-first-complete-set-interoperable-cloud-federation-to |title = The Contrail project is proud to present its first complete set of interoperable Cloud federation tools |archive-date = 2013-10-17 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131017190902/http://www.isgtw.org/announcement/contrail-project-proud-present-its-first-complete-set-interoperable-cloud-federation-to |last = Versweyveld |first = Leslie |date = 30 October 2012 |website = International Science Grid This Week (ISGTW) |access-date = 17 October 2013 |url-status = usurped }}</ref>
* [[CYCLADES]], pioneered the use of [[Datagram|datagrams]], [[Protocol layering|functional layering]], and the [[End-to-end principle|end-to-end strategy]], concepts adopted in [[TCP/IP]] and the [[Internet]].<ref name="Abbatep3">{{harvnb|Abbate|1999|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=9BfZxFZpElwC&pg=PA3 3] "The manager of the ARPANET project, Lawrence Roberts, assembled a large team of computer scientists ... and he drew on the ideas of network experimenters in the United States and the United Kingdom. Cerf and Kahn also enlisted the help of computer scientists from England, France and the United States"}}</ref><ref name="Bennett2009">{{cite web |last1=Bennett |first1=Richard |date=September 2009 |title=Designed for Change: End-to-End Arguments, Internet Innovation, and the Net Neutrality Debate |url=https://www.itif.org/files/2009-designed-for-change.pdf |access-date=11 September 2017 |publisher=Information Technology and Innovation Foundation |pages=7, 11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=9 November 2020 |title=Between Stanford and Cyclades, a transatlantic perspective on the creation of Internet |url=https://www.inria.fr/en/between-stanford-and-cyclades-transatlantic-perspective-creation-internet |access-date=2023-09-04 |website=Inria}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{cite web |date=27 October 2009 |title=The Computer History Museum, SRI International, and BBN Celebrate the 40th Anniversary of First ARPANET Transmission, Precursor to Today's Internet |url=https://www.sri.com/newsroom/press-releases/computer-history-museum-sri-international-and-bbn-celebrate-40th-anniversary |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190329134941/https://www.sri.com/newsroom/press-releases/computer-history-museum-sri-international-and-bbn-celebrate-40th-anniversary |archive-date=March 29, 2019 |access-date=25 September 2017 |publisher=SRI International |quote=But the ARPANET itself had now become an island, with no links to the other networks that had sprung up. By the early 1970s, researchers in France, the UK, and the U.S. began developing ways of connecting networks to each other, a process known as internetworking.}}</ref>
* [[Eigen (C++ library)]]
* [[Esterel]], a [[programming language]] for State Automata
* Geneauto — code-generation from model<ref>{{cite web|url=http://forge.scilab.org/index.php/p/geneauto-p/|title=Geneauto / P toolset - The P toolset includes a code generation and verification framework for the languages supported by the TOPCASED environment|publisher=[[Scilab]]}}</ref>
* Graphite, a research platform for computer graphics, 3D modeling and numerical geometry
* Gudhi — A [[C++]] library with [[Python (programming language)|Python]] interface for [[computational topology]] and [[topological data analysis]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://gudhi.gforge.inria.fr/|title=Gudhi, INRIA}}</ref>
* [[Le Lisp]], a portable Lisp implementation
* medInria, a medical image processing software, popularly used for MRI images.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://med.inria.fr/|title=medInria}}</ref>
* [[GNU MPFR]], an arbitrary-precision floating-point library
* [[OpenVibe|OpenViBE]], a [[software platform]] dedicated to designing, testing and using [[brain–computer interface]]s.
* [[Pharo]], an open-source Smalltalk derived from [[Squeak (programming language)|Squeak]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pharo.org|title=Pharo}}</ref>
* [[Rocq]], a [[proof assistant]]
* [[scikit-learn]], a machine learning software package
* [[Scilab]], a numerical computation software package
* [[SimGrid]]
* [[SmartEiffel]], a free Eiffel compiler
* [[Simulation Open Framework Architecture|SOFA]], an open source framework for multi-physics simulation with an emphasis on medical simulation.
* [[Tom (pattern matching language)|TOM]], a pattern matching language
* ViSP, an open source visual servoing platform library 
* [[XtreemFS]]<ref name="ISGTW" />
*  XtreemOS, a grid distributed operating system
* Zenon, an extensible automated theorem prover producing checkable proofs

Inria furthermore leads French AI Research, ranking 12th worldwide in 2019, based on accepted publications at the [[Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://medium.com/@dcharrezt/neurips-2019-stats-c91346d31c8f|title=NeurIPS 2019 Stats|date=18 December 2019 }}</ref>

== History ==
During the summer of 1988, the INRIA connected its Sophia-Antipolis unit to the [[NSFNet]] via [[Princeton University|Princeton]] using a satellite link leased to France Telecom and MCI. The link became operational on 8 August 1988, and allowed INRIA researchers to access the US network and allowed [[NASA]] researchers access to an astronomical database based in [[Strasbourg]]. This was the first international connection to NSFNET and the first time that French networks were connected directly to a network using [[TCP/IP]]. The [[Internet in France]] was limited to research and education for some years to come.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |title=The Routledge Companion to Global Internet Histories |date=2017 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1317607656 |pages=84–89 |chapter=The path to digital literacy and network culture in France (1980s to 1990s) |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TzslDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA84}}</ref><ref>''Et Dieu crea l'Internet'', Christian Huitema, {{ISBN|2-212-08855-8}}, 1995, page 10</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Andrianarisoa |first=Menjanirina |title=A brief history of the internet |date=2 March 2012 |url=http://thetechnologytrend.blogspot.com/2012/03/brief-history-of-internet.html}}</ref>
